claim: JNU wrote to Delhi Police asking them to take utmost precautions before entering the campus, and police officers told the university they would enter only if absolutely necessary under the law and that authorities would be informed in advance.

sources.originates_from: JNU status report to the HRD ministry, as reported

notes: Single secondary source (Onmanorama, 15 February 2016, reporting JNU's status report to the HRD ministry, confirmed by the Registrar per the article). The letter and the report have not been seen. Compare HIST-JNU16-006, which reports a letter giving permission. Both letters are reported and neither has been read.

claim: Police were deployed on the University of Hyderabad campus on 22 March 2016, the day Vice-Chancellor Appa Rao Podile resumed charge after leave following the death of Rohith Vemula, and students and some faculty were removed from the area outside the Vice-Chancellor's lodge and taken into custody that day.
notes: Four independent accounts agree that police were on campus on 22 March and that students were detained that evening. Accounts differ on force used, numbers and cause. No finding on proportionality.

claim: The Registrar's Office notice stated that Prof. Appa Rao Podile 'resumed the charge in the Forenoon of March 22, 2016'.
notes: Quoted in a Round Table India chronology. The notice itself was not read.

claim: Chronology of 22 March 2016 as given by one writer: protesters reached the Vice-Chancellor's residence about 10:30; police arrived about 11:30; RAF and more police arrived about 12:30 and senior officers met the Vice-Chancellor; forcible eviction and lathi-charge began about 16:00; students and three faculty members were taken into custody about 18:00; messes were closed about 21:00.
notes: Single author's account with times given as reported. A student account in the same piece puts police strength at about 400 personnel and four trucks; that figure is unverified.

claim: Count of persons arrested and charged: police and prosecution accounts give 25 students and 2 faculty members (27 accused); the Newslaundry report of the Gachibowli remand diary gives 24 students, 2 faculty members and 1 documentary filmmaker, with 20 more students added to the FIR but not arrested; the Joint Action Committee for Social Justice gave 36 students including 3 professors picked up about 5 pm on 22 March; the Round Table India chronology gives 37 students and 3 faculty members.
notes: Four versions. The 27-accused figure appears at the bail hearing (Sabrang) and in the NHRC release as a media-reported figure. The 36 and 37 figures come from protest groups and a student account and may count people detained and released. The remand diary itself was not read. NHRC gives the arrests as the evening of 23 March; most other sources give 22 March for the detention and 23 March for production in court and remand.

claim: The Joint Action Committee for Social Justice (UoH) alleged that 36 students including 3 professors were detained about 5 pm on 22 March, beaten in a police van and held overnight at undisclosed locations, which it believed to include Miyapur and Narsing police stations.
notes: Allegation by the committee, not a finding. No police or government response appears in the article.

claim: The Independent Fact Finding Team alleged that 27 students and 2 faculty members were taken into police vans, beaten and held in undisclosed locations for more than 24 hours, and alleged beatings, abusive language and threats of rape and death.

sources.publication: Round Table India (republishing the Independent Fact Finding Team press statement, 26 March 2016)

notes: Team members named on the page: Henri Tiphagne, Asha Kowtal, Paul Divakar, Burnard Fatima, V A Ramesh Nathan, Tara Rao (Amnesty International India). Allegations of the team, not findings.

claim: Injuries: PUDR stated that over fifty students were injured; Newslaundry reported a Deputy Commissioner of Police as saying four police officers were injured by stone-pelting; the Round Table India chronology says two students were taken to the health centre at about 11:30 with more hospitalised later.

sources.publication: People's Union for Democratic Rights (press statement, 23 March 2016)

notes: No official injury count, hospital record or medico-legal figure was found. The 'over fifty' figure is PUDR's allegation and its basis is not stated in the statement. Police describe the force used as mild and deny a lathi-charge, as reported by Newslaundry; protest groups describe a lathi-charge.

claim: Police account as reported: after two warnings police used 'mild force'; students allegedly pelted stones, injuring four officers; a lathi-charge and abuse of women students by male police were denied as 'wrongly reported in some media'.
notes: Attributed in the article to a Madhapur Deputy Commissioner of Police. The statement itself was not read. Opposed by the accounts in HIST-HCU-005, 006, 007 and 019.

claim: The Cyberabad Police Commissioner (reported as CV Anand) said of those arrested: 'They were all produced in Miyapur court and sent to judicial remand.'
notes: A statement about what happened after arrest. It does not say who ordered the deployment.

claim: On 28 March 2016 the XXV Metropolitan Magistrate court at Miyapur Court Complex granted bail to 27 accused (reported as 25 students and 2 faculty members), on surety, with a condition to report weekly to the Gachibowli Station House Officer. The public prosecutor did not oppose bail and was quoted as saying the arrests were made 'in order to control the situation'.
notes: Sabrang text is internally inconsistent on the surety amount (Rs 5,000 and Rs 50,000) and on 25 versus 27 students. Sections were described only as damage to public property, trespass, obstructing officials 'and other relevant sections of IPC'. The order and FIR were not read. Countercurrents (HIST-HCU-021) reports bail orders were reserved for 27 persons with hearing on 28 March, consistent with this.

claim: Two cases were registered at Gachibowli police station against protesting students and two faculty members, with charges reported as vandalism, rioting and criminal trespass.
notes: No FIR number, section list or text was found. Search for the FIR and the remand diary is an open task (RTI to Cyberabad Commissionerate, or copy from the Miyapur court).

claim: On 25 March 2016 the National Human Rights Commission took suo motu cognisance of media reports of an 'emergency like situation in Hyderabad University' and issued notices to the Secretary of the Union Ministry of Human Resource Development, the Chief Secretary of Telangana and the Police Commissioner, Hyderabad, seeking reports within one week.

sources.publication: National Human Rights Commission (press release, 25 March 2016)

notes: Primary document read (press release, 25 March 2016). The release records media reports of about 25 students and 2 faculty members arrested on the evening of 23 March, and states 'No one can be deprived of the basic amenities like water, food and electricity by willful act of the State.' It makes no finding on who ordered the police entry. The reports the notices produced were not found.

claim: The replies of the Union HRD Ministry, the Telangana Chief Secretary and the Hyderabad Police Commissioner to the NHRC notice of 25 March 2016, and any NHRC case file number or closure, were not found.
notes: Not located on the NHRC site or in news coverage. Task: NHRC HRCNet case search and RTI to NHRC for the case file.

claim: A writ petition by University of Hyderabad professor Tathagata Sengupta and student P. Adityan led the Hyderabad High Court to direct the Telangana government, in a hearing reported on 19 July 2016, to explain within ten days alleged unlawful police conduct on campus. The advocate said an ACP declined to accept a complaint against a fellow ACP who led the baton charge.
notes: The News Minute gives the campus date as 21 March 2016, which conflicts with 22 March in every other source and is probably an error. The case number, the order and any State counter-affidavit were not found. The article contains no statement from the State on who called the police.

claim: The State's counter-affidavit in the Sengupta and Adityan petition, and any order disposing of it, were not found.
notes: Under SOURCING.md this is the highest-value missing document on the order question. Task: Telangana High Court case status search and Indian Kanoon for the 2016 writ.

claim: Utilities and messes: students said water, electricity and internet were cut and all messes closed from 23 March 2016; a faculty statement says 14 hostel messes were shut for about 48 hours; the Round Table India chronology attributes to the Registrar the words 'Shut down the Messes and the Water facilities, all this protesting students will come to sense'.

sources.publication: Countercurrents.org (statement of SC and ST Faculty Forum and Concerned Teachers, 26 March 2016)
National Human Rights Commission (press release, 25 March 2016)

notes: The students' and faculty claims are allegations. The Registrar quote is an unnamed witness's report. The administration's reported position, seen in search results but not on a page read, is that the water shortage predated the protest and that miscreants damaged a pump. NHRC cites media reports of shortages of water, electricity, food and internet and does not attribute the cause. Who ordered any cut is not established.

The Independent Fact Finding Team interviewed the Cyberabad Deputy Commissioner, an Assistant Commissioner, an Inspector of Police and the Telangana State Home Minister; its published statement and interim report do not record what any of them said about who requested or ordered police entry onto campus.

notes: The interim report lists the police officer met as a DCP and says a more detailed report will follow. That fuller report was not found. The Vice-Chancellor declined an interview and the team was refused entry to campus.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The fact-finding interim report alleges that the Vice-Chancellor's return to campus was planned with supporters and triggered the violence, and that the Home Minister and police had advised him against returning.
notes: Allegation by the team as summarised by Sabrang. The advice by the Home Minister and police is not documented elsewhere in what was found. This would place a state-government office as having advised against the return, which is different from ordering the entry.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. A Kafila guest post by HCU students states that the CRPF and RAF were 'called in at the behest of the Vice Chancellor Appa Rao'.

sources.publication: Kafila (guest post by HCU students, 23 March 2016)

notes: Student allegation, undated beyond 23 March 2016, with no document cited. Treated as an allegation against the Vice-Chancellor's office.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The Joint Action Committee for Social Justice alleged that police, RAF and CRPF acted 'upon the orders of the Central and state government', and that media reports said police had a list of students and faculty supplied by the Vice-Chancellor.
notes: Allegation without a cited order. The article does not say which media reports. No government response is quoted. The Union government's role is not documented in any source read.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. A faculty statement says security staff 'had been ordered to bar outsiders from entering' the campus, without saying by whom, and that the administration justified the arrests as 'a crack-down on vandals'.

notes: Newslaundry does not say who signed the letter or whether it was sent before or after police took over the campus. The letter was not seen. This is a request about access by outsiders and is not shown to be a request for police to enter the campus or to detain students.

It does not show who then ordered deployment or detention. The three police officers are named in the article; this entry does not repeat names because the document itself was not read.

notes: Single source. If a complaint was registered it would be a document (GD entry or complaint copy) obtainable from Gachibowli police station. Not found.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The public prosecutor told the Miyapur court that 'the arrest were made by the police in order to control the situation' on 22 March.
notes: A court-room statement of the prosecution at the bail hearing as reported by Sabrang. It speaks to the purpose of the arrests, not to who ordered them.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. Who gave the order to bring police and central forces onto the campus and to detain students on 22 March 2016 is not established by any primary document found. No deployment order, requisition, request letter, station diary entry, FIR, affidavit, inquiry report or court order was located naming the office or person.
notes: Candidate offices on the record: the university administration (letter on access to Cyberabad police; task sheet; staff complaint; student allegations), the Cyberabad Police Commissionerate (statements after the fact; the officers on the ground), the Telangana government (Home Minister interviewed by the fact-finding team; alleged advice against the VC's return; NHRC notice to Chief Secretary), and the Union government (alleged by a protest group, CRPF and RAF involvement alleged; no document). None is established.

claim: The Vice-Chancellor had a registered case against him under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act in connection with Rohith Vemula's death, on which, according to the fact-finding team, no action had been taken when he returned.
notes: As stated in the interim report. The FIR (Cyberabad, January 2016) was not read. Context for the protest, no finding on its merits.

claim: Procedure after detention: the fact-finding team said those arrested were not produced before a magistrate within 24 hours and that police could have given bail but the students and faculty were remanded; the faculty statement says production at Miyapur court and remand to 14 days' judicial custody followed.

sources.publication: Countercurrents.org (statement of SC and ST Faculty Forum and Concerned Teachers, 26 March 2016)

notes: The Cyberabad Commissioner is reported as saying the accused were produced at Miyapur court and remanded. Whether production met the 24-hour rule depends on the time of arrest, which sources put at about 17:00 to 18:00 on 22 March, with remand late on 23 March. The remand order and arrest memos were not read.

claim: Police used force, including a lathicharge, against protesting students at Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi, on the night of 23 September 2017. Press reports say women students, at least two journalists and some police personnel were injured.
notes: Occurrence is consistent across sources. The Vice-Chancellor denied that students were lathicharged on campus (see HIST-BHU-012). Location of the force (campus gates, women's hostel area, outside campus) differs between accounts and is not resolved here.

claim: Students began protesting at BHU after 21 September 2017, when a woman student said she was harassed by three men on a motorcycle inside the campus. Students alleged that when she complained at the Proctor's office she was shamed and told not to go out after 6 pm. The allegation about the Proctor's office is the students' and is not a finding.
notes: Newslaundry gives the 21 September timeline; Outlook describes the harassment allegation. Neither shows a document from the university.

claim: The Varanasi Divisional Commissioner submitted a report to the Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary on or about 26 September 2017. As reported by IANS, it said BHU did not deal with the victim's complaint in a sensitive manner or in time, and called the administration's failure 'the biggest fault'. The reports do not say the report examined who ordered the police action.
notes: The report itself was not found or read. The three outlets relay the same findings; IANS appears to be the common origin, so these are not three independent sources. Chief Minister asked for this report on 24 or 25 September (see HIST-BHU-009).

claim: Who gave the order for the lathicharge on the night of 23 September 2017 is not established in any document or report retrieved. No order, police log, magistrate's direction or inquiry finding naming the office that authorised the use of force was found.
notes: Sources read are silent on the point: Outlook (25 and 26 September 2017), Newslaundry, The Quint, National Herald, Tribune. Documents that would settle it: Varanasi district magistrate's and police commissionerate or SSP's records of the deployment and any direction to disperse, Lanka police station general diary, the magisterial inquiry report, the state judicial inquiry report, and BHU's record of any request for police help. The BHU spokesperson was reported saying 'police help had been sought' (Outlook, 25 September 2017) without saying who sought it or from whom.

claim: On 24 September 2017 journalists protesting in Lucknow demanded action against the Varanasi District Magistrate and the Senior Superintendent of Police 'for ordering the lathicharge'. This is the journalists' allegation as reported. The same report describes the two officers meeting university officers and does not say they ordered anything.
notes: Single source, and it attributes the order only through the protesters' demand. The offices (District Magistrate, SSP) are named in the source with individual names; those names are omitted here because no primary document was read that ties them to the order. Not a finding.

claim: Between 24 and 25 September 2017 the Varanasi district administration and police removed from their posts three additional city magistrates, the station officer of Lanka police station and the circle officer of Bhelupur, reported as 'in connection with the lathicharge'. Dynamite News and Aaj Tak say the officials were found prima facie responsible for the lathicharge. The reports do not name the authority that issued the removal order.
notes: Outlook reproduces a district information office release for the magistrates and police sources for the police officers. The release was not itself read. Reports differ on numbers: Aaj Tak and Dynamite list one additional city magistrate, the Lanka station officer and the Bhelupur circle officer; Outlook lists three magistrates (see HIST-BHU-007). A removal is an administrative step and is not a finding that any of them gave the order.

claim: Reports differ on how many officials were removed. Outlook (25 September 2017) lists three additional city magistrates plus the Lanka station officer and the Bhelupur circle officer. Aaj Tak (25 September 2017) lists one additional city magistrate plus those two police officers. The Tribune (27 September 2017) says three additional city magistrates and three policemen. Outlook's 26 September piece says two police officers.
notes: Versions kept side by side. Resolution needs the district information office release or the government order itself.

claim: Police registered an FIR against unidentified policemen over the lathicharge of 23 September 2017 and a separate case against over 1,000 students over the violence, announced on 25 September 2017 at Lanka police station per PTI.
notes: FIR texts, sections and complainants were not found. PTI is the common origin of both outlets.

claim: The number of students named in the case differs between reports: over 1,000 (PTI via Outlook and Eastern Mirror, 25 September 2017) and 1,200 unidentified students (Aaj Tak, 25 September 2017).
notes: Only the FIR would settle the figure.

claim: The number of people injured on 23 September 2017 is not established. Reports say only 'a number of students, including women, and two journalists' were injured, and that some police personnel were hurt per police sources. No source retrieved gives a count.
notes: Hospital admission and medico-legal figures were not found. Consent and privacy limits apply to individual medical records; aggregate hospital figures could be sought by RTI.

claim: Detentions reported: 16 detained students were released on the evening of 24 September 2017, per the Lanka station officer quoted by PTI via Outlook. Over 200 Samajwadi Party activists were detained while trying to reach the injured students, and Congress leaders were detained and later released while heading to BHU. No total number of students detained on the night of 23 September is given.
notes: Several of these detentions are of political workers on 24 and 25 September, not of students on the night of the lathicharge.

claim: Vice-Chancellor Girish Chandra Tripathi denied, as reported on 26 September 2017, that students were lathicharged on campus. He said action was taken against people who threw petrol bombs and stones and tried to burn property, and that police used force only to move such elements out of the campus. He also described the protest as created by outsiders and said it was staged before the Prime Minister's visit. These are his statements as reported.
notes: Statements attributed to the Vice-Chancellor by IANS, NDTV (via National Herald) and Outlook. They do not say who ordered the police to act.

claim: On 24 and 25 September 2017 the Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister ordered a probe and sought a report from the Divisional Commissioner, Varanasi; the Varanasi district administration ordered a magisterial inquiry into the four days of incidents including the lathicharge; and a state judicial inquiry was announced. Outlook also reports a committee under the Chief Secretary.
notes: The orders constituting these inquiries were not read. Outcomes of the magisterial and state judicial inquiries were not found.

claim: The BHU Vice-Chancellor ordered a judicial inquiry led by a retired Allahabad High Court judge, reported on 26 September 2017 after an executive council meeting. The judge's name is given as V K Dixit by The Tribune and Morung Express and as B S Dixit by Outlook.
notes: Judge's name differs across sources; the order was not read. This is a university inquiry, separate from the state's.

claim: The BHU inquiry committee headed by a former High Court judge released its findings on 25 April 2018, per The Wire's LiveWire. It is reported to have given the Vice-Chancellor a clean chit and to have described the protest as 'politicised and sponsored'.
notes: Single source and an opinion-leaning piece. The report text was not found. Not read for what it says about who ordered the police action. Treat as unverified until the report is obtained.

claim: BHU Chief Proctor O N Singh resigned on 26 September 2017, reported as taking 'moral responsibility' for the molestation of a student and the police violence that followed. The Tribune attributes no direct quote to him.
notes: Resignation is reported as a fact; the reason is the press's description. No document names the Proctor as having requested or ordered police action.

claim: Vice-Chancellor Tripathi went on leave on 2 October 2017 citing personal reasons, and the BHU registrar was appointed interim Vice-Chancellor on 4 October 2017, per The Quint's live blog.
notes: Single dated source.

claim: The National Human Rights Commission sought a detailed report on the incident from the Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary, the Director General of Police and the Vice-Chancellor within four weeks, per The Quint.
notes: NHRC case number and notice were not found. Replies, if filed, would be primary evidence on the chain of command.

claim: Aaj Tak reports (25 September 2017) that the Prime Minister and the BJP president spoke to the Chief Minister and asked him to take necessary steps. Outlook says 'reportedly'. This is a press account of a conversation and is not a direction about the lathicharge.
notes: Sourcing of the conversation is not given in either article.

claim: No Allahabad High Court order, petition or commission report on the BHU events of 21 to 24 September 2017 was found in this research.
notes: Searches of news coverage returned no High Court proceeding. Indian Kanoon and the eCourts portal were not searched in this pass and should be before concluding no case exists. The only judge-led inquiry found is the university's (HIST-BHU-014).

claim: Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel entered the Jamia Millia Islamia campus in the evening of 15 December 2019 and used force and tear gas there. The Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 records, from the NHRC's findings, that protesters pushed back by police entered the campus 'following which the police also entered the campus' (para 81), and that the use of tear-gas shells inside the library 'could have been avoided' (paras 18, 42, 83).

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020

notes: The occurrence is established by a court judgment that recites the NHRC's findings and by the police's own account to a magistrate (secondary report of the action taken report). The court makes no finding that any individual officer acted unlawfully and says its conclusion is not an approval of every act attributed to police (para 92). Time of entry is DISPUTED between sources: the petitioners' case in the judgment (para 12) says about 4:00 p.m.; Wikipedia (tertiary, not independently checked) says 6:46 p.m. The judgment does not fix a time.

claim: On 13 December 2019 a march by Jamia students towards Parliament was stopped near the campus. The petitioners' case, as recited in the Delhi High Court judgment, is that at about 3:00 p.m. police resorted to tear-gas shelling in the vicinity of the campus and several students were injured. LiveLaw's account of the NHRC report says the 13 December 'clash' was contained at Gate No. 1 and that no complaint was made to any authority about it.

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: The judgment (para 11) states this as the petitioners' case, not as a finding. Wikipedia (tertiary) says 50 students were detained on 13 December; that count was not checked against its cited news sources and is not repeated as established. No document read here says who gave any order on 13 December. The 13 December events are far less documented than 15 December.

claim: Who gave the order to enter the campus on 15 December 2019: NOT ESTABLISHED. No document read for this record names the person or the office that ordered the entry. The Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 describes the entry as an act of 'the police' and names no officer or rank. The police's action taken report (16 March 2020), as reported by Scroll.in and The Quint, says police were 'forced to enter' and names no officer. The Home Ministry's written Lok Sabha reply of 4 February 2020, as reported by The Leaflet, says police entered 'chasing the violent congregation of students/ mob' and names no officer.

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020
Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020
Written reply by MoS (Home) G. Kishan Reddy in the Lok Sabha, reported 4 February 2020

notes: Level of office: the only institution all sources attribute the entry to is the Delhi Police (with Rapid Action Force personnel, para 18 of the judgment). The rank at which the decision was taken (station, district, range, headquarters, or the Union Home Ministry, to which Delhi Police reports) is unknown. The judgment records no police counter-affidavit statement naming a commander. The NHRC report (read only through summaries) is also reported as naming no one. The Deputy Commissioner of Police (Southeast) is named in a Scroll.in report only as an official who declined to comment on the firing inquiry; no document says he gave any order and this archive makes no such claim. Documents that could settle it are listed at HIST-JMI-020 to HIST-JMI-023.

claim: Who gave the order to use tear gas, including inside the library: NOT ESTABLISHED. The Delhi Police action taken report, as reported, says officials 'used tear gas shells and moderate force to disperse the protestors' and names no authorising officer. The NHRC found, as recorded in the Delhi High Court judgment, that the use of tear-gas shells inside the library 'could have been avoided'. LiveLaw's and The Wire's summaries of the NHRC report say it called the tear gas 'an irresponsible action of the police' and recommended action against those who used it.

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020
NHRC report, as summarised by The Wire on 26 June 2020 (the report itself was not read)
NHRC report, as summarised by LiveLaw on 27 June 2020 (the report itself was not read)

notes: The NHRC recommendation of action against personnel who used tear gas in the library is reported by two outlets, but the report itself was not read and no action against any identified officer has been found (see HIST-JMI-018). Whether the tear gas was fired on an order from a supervisor or on individual decision is not stated in any document read.

claim: Who gave the order to use lathis or other force against students, and who ordered detentions: NOT ESTABLISHED. The Delhi Police action taken report, as reported, says students were 'temporarily apprehended' under section 65 of the Delhi Police Act and evacuated 'hands up'.
